item.title: Bill proposes $3m campaign spending cap for political parties
item.description: Political parties would be limited to spending $3 million on an election campaign, while individual candidates would face a $300,000 spending cap, under a Bill tabled in Parliament today. The Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) (Amendment) Bill 2026 proposes new campaign expenditure limits applying to political parties, party candidates and independent candidates.
item.content:encoded:
Political parties would be limited to spending $3 million on an election campaign, while individual candidates would face a $300,000 spending cap, under a Bill tabled in Parliament today.

The Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) (Amendment) Bill 2026 proposes new campaign expenditure limits applying to political parties, party candidates and independent candidates.

Under the proposed new section 24, the limits would apply from the first day of the campaign period until the 60th day after polling day.

“A candidate (whether an independent candidate or a political party candidate) must not spend more than $300,000 on his or her election campaign,” the Bill states.

It says a political party “must not spend more than $3,000,000 on its election campaign”.

The proposed spending limits would cover more than expenditure made during the official campaign period.

Any income pledged or expenditure incurred outside the prescribed period for use during the campaign period would also count towards the spending ceiling.

The Bill also specifically addresses traditional or protocol gifts made when campaigning in villages and communities.

Any gift given by a candidate or political party to a village or community group as protocol, or for a similar purpose, solely to obtain permission to enter its territory would count towards campaign expenditure and would have to be declared.

However, the Bill states that such a gift, when properly declared under section 25, would not constitute bribery under section 140 of the Electoral Act 2014.

Breaching the proposed $300,000 candidate limit or $3 million political party limit would be classified as a corrupt electoral practice.

The explanatory note says the introduction of campaign expenditure limits is intended to “create a level playing field for all political parties and candidates.”

The Bill forms part of proposed changes to the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) Act 2013.

item.title: Bill proposes $100,000 fine for corrupt electoral practices
item.description: Political parties could face fines of up to $100,000 for corrupt electoral practices under proposed amendments to Fiji’s Electoral Act 2014. The Electoral (Amendment) Bill 2026 introduces a new classification separating offences into “corrupt electoral practices” and “illegal electoral practices”, with different penalties applying to political parties, candidates, polling agents and other individu
item.content:encoded:
Political parties could face fines of up to $100,000 for corrupt electoral practices under proposed amendments to Fiji’s Electoral Act 2014.

The Electoral (Amendment) Bill 2026 introduces a new classification separating offences into “corrupt electoral practices” and “illegal electoral practices”, with different penalties applying to political parties, candidates, polling agents and other individuals.

Under proposed section 135A, a person who commits an offence classified as a corrupt electoral practice could face up to two years imprisonment, a fine, or both.

For corrupt electoral practices, the maximum fine would be $100,000 for a political party, $40,000 for a candidate or polling agent, and $10,000 in any other case.

A person convicted of a corrupt electoral practice would also be disqualified from registering on the National Register of Voters for four years.

The Bill proposes lower penalties for offences classified as illegal electoral practices.

These would carry maximum fines of $40,000 for a political party, $20,000 for a candidate or polling agent and $5,000 for any other person.

The proposed changes would also amend existing penalty provisions under sections 136, 137 and 138 of the Electoral Act.

Several offences which currently carry their own specified fines and imprisonment terms would instead be classified as either corrupt or illegal electoral practices and become subject to the penalties provided under the new section 135A.

Among the changes, provisions currently carrying penalties of up to $50,000 or 10 years imprisonment would have their existing penalty wording removed and be classified as corrupt electoral practices.

Other provisions currently carrying penalties including imprisonment of up to five years would instead be classified as illegal electoral practices.

The amendments form part of wider proposed changes to Fiji’s electoral laws contained in the Electoral (Amendment) Bill 2026 currently before Parliament.

item.title: Electoral amendment Bill tabled in Parliament
item.description: The Electoral (Amendment) Bill 2026 seeks to broaden participation in Fiji’s electoral process while strengthening the administration of elections and introducing clearer classifications for electoral offences. Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga told Parliament the proposed amendments would modernise Fiji’s electoral framework through changes to the Electoral Act 2014.
item.content:encoded:
The Electoral (Amendment) Bill 2026 seeks to broaden participation in Fiji’s electoral process while strengthening the administration of elections and introducing clearer classifications for electoral offences.

Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga told Parliament the proposed amendments would modernise Fiji’s electoral framework through changes to the Electoral Act 2014.

“The proposed amendments are designed to facilitate broader participation in the electoral process, improve the administration of elections [and] clearly define electoral offences through a new classification system of corrupt and illegal electoral practices,” Mr Turaga said.

He said the Bill also responded to issues identified during recent consultations on Fiji’s electoral laws.

Changes are also proposed to provisions governing election campaigns, postal voting and pre-poll voting.

Mr Turaga said these areas needed to be updated to better reflect current realities and support the efficient conduct of elections.

“It further updates campaign, postal voting and pre-poll voting provisions to better reflect realities and support the efficient conduct of elections,” he said.

Mr Turaga said the reforms were intended to strengthen Fiji’s electoral system and public confidence in democratic institutions.

“These amendments will contribute to a more accessible, transparent [and] accountable electoral system that strengthens public confidence in our democratic institutions,” he said.

item.title: Fiji Airways confirms recent jet fuel delivery cannot be used at Nadi Airport
item.description: A recent delivery of jet fuel to Nadi International Airport cannot presently be used, prompting Fiji Airways to secure alternative fuel supplies to maintain its flight operations. Fiji Airways confirmed the issue in a statement today, saying it was dealing with what it described as a “minor, temporary jet fuel supply constraint” at the country’s main international airport.
item.content:encoded:
A recent delivery of jet fuel to Nadi International Airport cannot presently be used, prompting Fiji Airways to secure alternative fuel supplies to maintain its flight operations.

Fiji Airways confirmed the issue in a statement today, saying it was dealing with what it described as a “minor, temporary jet fuel supply constraint” at the country’s main international airport.

The airline said the constraint followed a recent delivery from one of its fuel suppliers that could not currently be used.

“Safety remains Fiji Airways’ absolute priority, and the airline does not anticipate any disruption to flights or guests, having already secured alternative fuel supplies,” the airline said.

Fiji Airways did not provide further details in the statement on why the latest fuel delivery could not be used.

The airline said it was working with relevant government agencies, Fiji Airports Limited and other industry partners to ensure operations continued smoothly.

It stressed that fuel would not be used until it had met the airline’s testing and clearance requirements.

“All fuel [is] subject to Fiji Airways’ rigorous testing and clearance requirements before use,” the airline said.

Despite the fuel supply constraint, Fiji Airways said it did not anticipate any disruption to its flights or passengers because alternative supplies had already been secured.

The development comes as stakeholders continue to closely monitor the aviation fuel situation at Nadi International Airport.

item.title: Fuel quality concerns monitored at Nadi Airport
item.description: Fiji Airports says aviation fuel quality and supply issues at Nadi International Airport are being handled by fuel service providers and relevant authorities, as the airport closely monitors the developing situation. In a statement to this newspaper, Fiji Airports said aviation fuel at Nadi International Airport was supplied and managed by the relevant fuel service providers.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji Airports says aviation fuel quality and supply issues at Nadi International Airport are being handled by fuel service providers and relevant authorities, as the airport closely monitors the developing situation.

In a statement to this newspaper, Fiji Airports said aviation fuel at Nadi International Airport was supplied and managed by the relevant fuel service providers.

“Matters relating to fuel quality, availability and supply are therefore being addressed by those providers in coordination with the relevant authorities, while Fiji Airports continues to support the safe and continuous operation of the airport,” the statement said.

Fiji Airports said Nadi International Airport remained open and operational, with established safety and operational protocols being maintained.

The airport operator said it was working closely with airlines, fuel suppliers, ground handling providers and other relevant stakeholders.

“Our primary responsibility is to support the safe and orderly operation of the airport, closely monitor fuel availability and expected supply, and assess any potential impacts on airport and airline operations,” it said.

“Where required, Fiji Airports is supporting stakeholders with appropriate contingency and operational planning to minimise disruption to passengers and flight operations.”

It said individual airlines continued to manage their own operational and fuel requirements in line with their procedures and regulatory obligations.

Fiji Airports said its immediate focus was on maintaining safe airport operations, coordinating with relevant parties and ensuring accurate and timely information was provided as the situation developed.

“Fiji Airports understands the concern this situation may cause passengers and the travelling public and acknowledges the inconvenience that any resulting operational adjustments may create.”

It said it would continue monitoring developments and support efforts to restore normal fuel supply arrangements as soon as practicable.

item.title: Fiji fuel contamination issue hits Virgin, Qantas, services
item.description: Airlines servicing Fiji are being forced to fly in fuel to the island nation as a fuel contamination issue hits the country’s international airport. Virgin Australia yesterday cancelled two services on its Fiji route and confirmed planes are being forced to stop halfway at airports such in New Caledonia and Vanuatu to make the journey back to Australia and Fiji.
item.content:encoded:
Airlines servicing Fiji are being forced to fly in fuel to the island nation as a fuel contamination issue hits the country’s international airport.

Virgin Australia yesterday cancelled two services on its Fiji route and confirmed planes are being forced to stop halfway at airports such in New Caledonia and Vanuatu to make the journey back to Australia and Fiji.

In what one pilot described to the ABC as a “very rare” situation, airlines are being asked to fuel up at alternative airports if possible and bring in stockpiles of fuel to Nadi International Airport.

In correspondence seen by the ABC, pilots are being told that there is a “major contamination” and supply cannot be guaranteed in Fiji.

Pilots have been told the problem may continue until the end of the month.

One pilot said he has to bring in “more than 20 tonnes” of fuel to Fiji in order to make the flight back to Australia.

On a standard plane that services Fiji that equates to about one third to a quarter of a tank.

Qantas said it had switched to larger planes, a Boeing 737 to an Airbus A330, for the Sydney-Nadi route to avoid needing to refuel in Nadi.

Sources have told the ABC the contamination issue relates to an excessive electrical charge in a batch of fuel stored at the airport, however it was unclear where the issue originated from.

The source indicated it could be resolved soon or escalate into a more significant issue.

Fiji Airports did not confirm the cause of the contamination issue.

A spokesperson said they were making “operational adjustments” and the airport was “closely monitoring the current aviation fuel situation”.

“Nadi International Airport remains open and operational, with established safety and operational protocols being maintained,” it said.

Virgin Airlines generally operates six flights a day to and from Fiji, from Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne. It cancelled two flights yesterday, one to Fiji from Brisbane and its returning flight.

According to tracking sites, flights so far today are scheduled to continue.

A Virgin spokesman described the contamination as a “temporary fuel issue”.

“We understand more fuel has arrived into Nadi and is undergoing the standard testing and approval processes required before use,” the spokesperson said.

item.title: Bail denied for military officer
item.description: A Military officer charged with a case of alleged unlawful possession of illicit drugs as well as an additional charge of attempted bribery has been denied bail. Rusiate Cama Tawakilai, 44, made his first appearance before Magistrate Shageeth Somaratne facing a count each of unlawful possession of illicit drugs, attempted bribery and serious assault.
item.content:encoded:
A Military officer charged with a case of alleged unlawful possession of illicit drugs as well as an additional charge of attempted bribery has been denied bail.

Rusiate Cama Tawakilai, 44, made his first appearance before Magistrate Shageeth Somaratne facing a count each of unlawful possession of illicit drugs, attempted bribery and serious assault.

It is alleged that on August 19, Mr Tawakilai was stopped and searched by a team of officers on patrol in Delainavesi, whereby a zip lock plastic containing white crystals which later tested positive for methamphetamine was discovered.

Mr Tawakilai then allegedly offered $150 to the arresting officer to release him, before fleeing the scene whereby he was arrested by two officers.

Mr Tawakilau sought bail on the grounds that his four children depend on him. However, police prosecution opposed bail, citing the public interest and the seriousness of the case.

After hearing submissions from both parties, Magistrate Somaratne refused bail.

Mr Tawakilai will appear on August 25 before Magistrate Sufia Hamza for his formal bail application.

item.title: Beqa farmer rebuilds his life through the land
item.description: In Dakuni Village, in the district of Sawau on Beqa Island, Eroni Dolodoi has cultivated more than just crops — he has cultivated a second chance. The 45-year-old farmer believes the land saved his life.
item.content:encoded:
In Dakuni Village, in the district of Sawau on Beqa Island, Eroni Dolodoi has cultivated more than just crops — he has cultivated a second chance.

The 45-year-old farmer believes the land saved his life.

In 2003, Eroni was imprisoned for three years, an experience that could easily have defined his future. Instead, he chose to let it reshape him.

Upon returning home, he turned to farming, determined to rebuild his life with dignity and purpose.

“The land is our greatest gift,” he said.

“It can change your life if you are willing to work it.”

Today, his farm reflects careful planning and perseverance.

His dalo is planted in staggered six, five and three-month cycles, while his yaqona is cultivated in six, four and three-month stages to ensure continuous production throughout the year.

The Ministry of Agriculture and Waterways recognised his commitment through its 2025–2026 Yaqona Program, providing him with an $8000 farmhouse to support his farming operations.

For Eroni, the small building represents far more than shelter.

“It gave me hope. It showed me that people believed I could make something of my life.”

His days are now spent tending crops, maintaining his farm and providing for his family.

The routine, he says, has given him the discipline that once seemed out of reach, while the soil has offered him a sense of belonging.

But his greatest harvest may be the message he shares with young people and former prisoners across Fiji.

“Do not waste your freedom. There is land — make use of it. The soil is waiting for your hands,” he said.

“Farming will give you dignity, discipline and a future. If I can rise again after prison, so can you.”

Eroni hopes his journey reminds others that mistakes do not have to become lifelong identities.

“Mistakes may mark a chapter,” he said, “but choices write the story.”

His choice was to return to the land — and in doing so, he found redemption.
